segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All across the country this month college freshmen are starting their new lives at their new schools. And it is so hard to get into so many schools these days. At Columbia University in New York City, 33,000 people applied. 31,000 were rejected. That is fewer than 7% getting in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the students who did get in, the students who made it here, they still wonder how they did it. You know, it was so hard to get here, what was it that worked? And they have their theories.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I think it's because my application was very focused on physics, and especially females in physics, because obviously that's a problem.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I had decent SAT scores, and I had a good GPA, but I think a big part of it was my essays.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: These Columbia students talked to reporter Phia Bennin. On their very first day on campus, it was obvious who is a freshman because they all had to wear neon bracelets, like they were at a waterpark.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, I've been a competitive gymnast for my entire life.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I was a rhythmic gymnast, and I competed for the US national team.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I don't know. I'm pretty diverse, I guess-- Hispanic, disabled, good grades.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I'm an Eagle Scout. That might have helped too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But you do not have to talk to many kids or scratch the surface very far at all before you get this response to the question, what got you into this school?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I have no idea.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I still actually have no clue whatsoever.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Just the percentage of people that get in is just absolutely minuscule, so it's just what the admissions officers see in you. And I have no idea what they saw. [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Phia Bennin
segments.text: You have no idea what?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I totally relate to that. I remember I was completely clueless when it came to applying to college-- what to do to get in, what to say on the essays to convince them that I was worthy of their schools. And even more basic than that, I really had no idea what would possibly make one school better than another, how to figure out what schools I should apply to. It was overwhelming.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And today on our show-- it's September, it's back to school-- we have stories of some of the most boneheaded things people try to do to get into college, plus the truly incredible story of how one man made it into college. That story from writer, Michael Lewis. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act one, "The Old College Try." So here at our radio show, we went looking for a college admissions officer who would tell us the most misguided things that people do when they're applying to schools. And we found Rick Clark, who's director of undergraduate admissions at the Georgia Institute of Technology, better known as Georgia Tech. And he said that he and his team are regularly getting emails and phone calls from parents who are pretending to be their own kids. And he sent me some of these emails with the names redacted.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You forwarded an email like this to us. This is from a mom's email address, and then it's signed from a son.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it says, "I was impressed by GT's beautiful campus and its close proximity to so many athletic teams and facilities in Atlanta. I look forward to speaking with someone from the business school. Thanks again for taking the time to meet with us on Saturday, and thanks for the awesome T-shirt." Now, the word awesome, is that the most common word that parents use to imitate their kids?

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: I'd say "awesome" and "cool." If they throw those in, I think they feel like they're covering their bases on impersonating a high school student. But ironically, I really almost never, in fact, see that in an email from a high school student.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ah. So Duplicitous parents, please take note. And then on the phone, when the parents call on the phone, do they use the word "awesome?"

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: I actually just did hear from one of my staff members who said they talked to a mom the other day who clearly was trying to sound like her 17-year-old daughter, not so much in the language she was using, but masking her voice. About 15 minutes in, she started using "she" instead of "I," even saying, what if she-- I mean, I wanted to list more activities on the application?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Rick Clark says that one thing that has amped this up, all the parents getting in touch, is that lots of schools take into account whether a student shows something called demonstrated interest in their college, meaning, did they show up on campus? Did they write emails to the admissions office afterwards? Were they in touch?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Georgia Tech, he says, does not take that stuff into account, but parents do not seem to have gotten the memo on that. He forwarded me an email that a mom wrote to her kid, offering the kid $20 if the kid would email the admissions office, which might have been fine if she hadn't accidentally sent her email to the admissions office. And Rick Clark says that he gets where the parents are coming from. He is a parent himself. He wants to do everything he can for his kids.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: In fact, we've got a five-year-old right now on a waiting list for a charter school.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, so you have to deal with some admissions persons?

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: Yeah. I'm getting a little taste of my own medicine because my kid is seventh on this waiting list. And my wife the other day was like, we're going to call him every week and see where he is. I'm like, whoa, whoa, whoa. You are really flirting with the line between loving him and just really being a stalker here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you forwarded this email that you all got. And I guess I shouldn't have been surprised by this, but I've got to say, I didn't think it-- it's from somebody whose kid is not even applying to college. It says, "Dear sir or madam, my second grader--"

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I can barely finish this sentence. You know this email?

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: Yeah, absolutely.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: "My second grader has decided on a career in electrical engineering. He is leaning towards MIT, [LAUGHS] but I do not find them helpful and would prefer a southern culture."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I like that he's playing on your pride, on your southern pride. "Would you please tell me how to prepare him for admission? He will be an Eagle Scout by then and wants to go to the best school. Please advise."

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, apparently MIT needs to pay more attention to seven-year-olds in their admission process.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Rick Clark also sent me a bunch of college essays written by kids that they have gotten at Georgia Tech, again, with the names redacted. Turns out, one common mistake that kids make when they're writing their essays is that they're sending out so many applications, they leave the names of other schools in their essays to Georgia Tech.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: All right. This is one, in fact, in a, I don't know, 14-line short essay. They twice mention a wrong school name. "So after visiting the campus, reading the information brochure, and researching the university website, I understand and believe that Duke offers what I hope to gain from my college experience."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHING] They're writing to Georgia Tech.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: And then it skips down a couple lines. And this is what really blows me away, because there's four words here separating two school names. "I've chosen to apply early decision to Georgia Tech because I believe Duke is the ideal university for me."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Are there trends in what kids are writing about, the way you feel like you see little fads and you get sick of them?

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: Oh. Well, the age-old one that, I mean, again, pretty much anybody that you would interview who's been in college admission for any period of time would be-- you know, we just call it now the "mission trip" essay. And great to go on a mission trip, great to have a cultural experience, but inevitably the way it reads is so predictable.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: We flew down to somewhere in Central America, and we got off the plane. It was really hot. And we got on the bus. And 20 miles outside of the village, our bus broke down, but we got picked up by a chicken truck and taken into town. And then over the course of my time there, I went expecting to help others, but it was, in fact, me who was changed. And even just when you first start reading that essay, you're like, oh, here it comes again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Most college essays are pretty bad. Rick estimates that only one out of every 20 or so essays that he reads is any good at all, that is, 19 bad ones if you're counting at home. But he says that he and his colleagues believe that they themselves are partly to blame for the essay questions that they actually put onto the applications, questions that always get the same mundane, suck-uppy answers from kid, after kid, after kid. Colleges just market themselves so aggressively to so many people.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: There's a girl that lives just on our street, and she's a senior this year. And she brought me over the stack of mail that she got from schools. I mean, this was just the last two months worth of mail, and it had to be two feet tall. And opening those up, I mean, they do start to just-- you put your hand over the name of the school, and it could be any place.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's funny when you put it that way. It's almost like the schools are being as generic in what they're saying to the students as the students are to the schools.

segments.speaker: Rick Clark
segments.text: That's right. Nobody puts dead squirrels on the front of their college brochure. I mean, it's all football teams winning, beautiful sunny day, kids under a tree with a professor. I mean, that's every other page. It just runs together.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Rick Clark, director of admissions at Georgia Tech. Go Jackets.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act two, "My Ames is True." So Michael Lewis is a pretty well-known writer and reporter. His books, Moneyball, The Blind Side, and The Big Short were made into movies. His bestsellers about Wall Street include Liar's Poker and Flash Boys. But this particular story happens long before he was writing books. He was in seventh grade in New Orleans, trying to avoid reading them.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And the English teacher, Mr. Downer, asked us to write a book report on a novel called Johnny Tremain. And I went home and I looked at the book. And I noticed on the back-- there was this great book report with the book, and it was just on the back of the book.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, you mean a little summary?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Little summary. And I just copied it out and handed it in and [INAUDIBLE] with it. It came back with an A on it. And it says, "See me" on the top in big red ink. And I go to see Mr. Downer, and he says, that's plagiarism. Oh, my god. What's plagiarism?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You had never heard of it?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Never heard of it. And the concept was alien to me. I mean, I just thought it was an odd concept because you repeat what other people say all the time. I was just repeating what someone else said. It just seemed like a very intelligent thing to repeat. And I was telling him this. I thought I was saving us all a lot of trouble.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Saving us trouble, like?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: It'll save him the trouble of reading something really awful. And I wouldn't have to write a boring book report or even read the boring book. I was doing both of us a favor. And it seemed kind of counterintuitive to have to generate a thing that had already been done.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mr. Downer does not agree, and the middle school principal decides to expel Michael.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And at this point, do you understand what's wrong with what you've done?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: No, I'm indignant. I understand I'm supposed to feel it's wrong, but I don't feel it's wrong.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Michael Lewis says, by the way, if you are a seventh grader hearing us talk about this right now and you want to try this with one of his books in your classroom, you totally have his blessing. He wishes you the best, though he is pretty sure you're going to get the same results that he did. Anyway, ultimately, his parents get involved. Seventh grade Michael Lewis is not expelled from school.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: But what I have to do is write 100 times a phrase that Mr. Downer has written on the blackboard, "I will not plagiarize the work of others."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: The punishment is to plagiarize 100 times, over, and over, and over. And I didn't understand really the point of this because I thought, well, this is just plagiarizing again. And if this is the way they just want to show me that it's supposed to be harder work to plagiarize, that was it.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This has become one of the stories that Michael has found himself telling now and then over the years.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Every now and then, I wheel it out. And at some point, it occurred to me that the mere fact I like this story says an awful lot about me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so what does this one say about you?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Well, I think it rhymes with sort of my worldview and the general sense that authority is often absurd, a general sense that punishments often don't fit crimes, a general sense that often things that are supposed to be wrong don't actually feel wrong, and maybe they aren't as wrong as people say.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You know, we all have certain stories from our childhoods that we trot out from time to time, out of all the thousands of things that ever happened to us. And usually, it's not many stories that we'll actually trot out, right? And the choices that we make, you know, the selection that we make of which incidents we find ourselves telling people, it says so much about us and how we see the world, which ones we pick.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I bring all this up because the actual real story that Michael Lewis is here on the radio show today to report is a very good example of that. Of course, this is our "How I Got Into College" show, so this is the story of how one guy, named Emir Kamenica, got into college, but it's also an illustration of this other thing. Anyway, here's Michael.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: I think if I were telling you Emir's story, I'd probably just start at the very beginning, how he was born in Bosnia in 1978, how he grew up in Sarajevo with loving parents and a happy family. But it's his story, so let's let him tell it the way he tells it.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: All right. Well, I guess the natural place to start the story might just be the outset of the war. I was 13 at the time. The war, from my perspective, because I wasn't particularly paying attention to the political situation, comes truly out of nowhere. It's sort of one morning, you wake up expecting the world will look just the way it did yesterday, and instead there are these people in leather jackets with stockings on their heads and machine guns in their hands.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So the Serb troops hadn't gotten to his neighborhood yet. And one Sunday, his mother took Emir and his sister across the river to visit his great aunt. The walk was about a mile.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So when we realized this might not have been a good idea is that we start crossing this bridge, some shooting starts. And it's clear some people are shooting at us because you can see the bullets ricochet around. And we just kind of run.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: They managed to get to the other side of the bridge without getting shot, but they couldn't go back. And his dad was trapped back where they lived. The Serb troops ended up killing a lot of the men in Emir's old neighborhood and raping the women. But when Emir tells the story, he stresses just how lucky they were to get out, for example, how lucky they were to hitch a ride from two women, complete strangers, and to join a convoy of 5,000 Bosnian refugees, all of them women and children fleeing for the Croatian coast, how lucky it was that they owned a camper near the beach where they spent the summers, how lucky it was that it was May, when the weather was warm, how lucky they were even after the weather turned cold and their camper became uninhabitable.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Which was actually another pure, fortuitous coincidence. My mother happened to be in a market and ran across a woman who was my sister's homeroom teacher in Sarajevo.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: This woman happened to be moving to London and needed someone to watch her apartment, more good luck. Clearly, there was some bad luck too, but Emir doesn't mention it. I have to prod him to fill in the piece of the story he most obviously leaves out.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So let me stop you for a second.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Yeah. Sorry, go on.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: I was going to ask you, do you know exactly what happened to your father?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I don't know exactly what happened. What I do know is that a neighbor of ours, a person who lived in our high rise, he found my father's body on the street, and he took him to the local cemetery and buried him. So we at least do know where he is.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Anyway, Emir and his mom and his sister moved into this apartment in a city crawling with hostile Croat nationalists. His mother wasn't allowed to work. And before long, Emir and his sister weren't allowed to go to school.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: When he went outside, Emir would be chased by these thugs who wanted to beat him up just because he was Muslim. His family wasn't even faintly religious, so he thought this was especially bizarre. He was stuck inside this apartment. In his telling, he did almost nothing but read books.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So I would get the books from the local library. I would sort of run there to make sure I don't encounter any of the nationalists that are trying to prove their patriotism by beating me up.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And I'm trying to picture this, actually. So you're actually running through the streets with library books under your arms and running back with other library books under your arms?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Yeah. It was library books. I also tried to teach myself a few things. Because eventually, you get bored of reading novels, so I tried to learn some more physics. I read a lot of Freud, which I decided was not that good.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: And one of the books I read was called The Fortress, by an author called Mesa Selimovic. And I do not know why. I guess, 15, I was impressionable. I was very much moved by that novel.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: I've never actually read The Fortress. But according to the description on the back of the book, it's about a young man who, quote, "overcomes the psychological anguish of war, only to find that he has emerged a reflective and contemplative man in a society that does not value the subversive implications of these qualities." Emir loved the book. He read it over and over.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: One day, his mother announces that they'd had another lucky break. Out of a million Bosnian refugees, they are among the first few thousand being handed tickets to the United States. They packed to leave, but all Emir has is some T-shirts, blue jeans, and this library book.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Which is still in my room. And so when we're packing to leave, I decide to bring it with me to the US as my most prized possession.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So when you take this book, are you sensitive to the fact you're stealing a library book?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I am entirely aware of that, yeah. I didn't feel like the community or the town had treated me very nicely, so I perhaps had less guilt than I might have in other circumstances.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: The UN dropped Emir and his mom and his sister in Atlanta, which was as good as any other place since they didn't know a soul in the entire country. They were picked up at the Atlanta airport along with an older Bosnian couple they don't know at all and taken to their new home.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: And we pull into this apartment complex. And I remember very well when the van stopped, I just saw this look of terror on my mother and sister's faces. So I immediately turned to them, reassuring, said, oh, no, no, no. They're not dropping us off here. This is just where this couple is going. We're going elsewhere.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So the guy opened the door. The other couple got out. And I just sort of, with my hand, signaled to my mother and sister to sit still because surely, surely this is not where we're going. But in fact, that was where we were going, and it's just horrible. There's cockroaches running all over the place.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So far as he could tell, there weren't any other white people in the neighborhood. And to Emir, this whole black people, white people thing was an entirely new experience. But the first thing that struck him was that the black people didn't really seem to like the white people very much.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Which was particularly ironic, given that, first, I don't know that I'm Muslim. All of a sudden, people try and kill me because they think I'm Muslim. I did not know I was white. Now, all of a sudden, these kids want to beat me up because I'm white.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Once again, he couldn't leave his home without feeling a little bit scared, even when he went to school, which was called Clarkston High. Sitting in his literature class one day, Emir heard a kid get shot right outside the classroom.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: The teacher was reading out loud from Romeo and Juliet at the time. I'm not sure if others noticed the kind of appropriateness. There was lots of racial tension. I was one of, I would guess, like 12 or 20 white kids in a school of 900. There were lots of fights, lots of fighting.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Probably the worst class of all, by far, was this biology class. And the teacher there-- this was, I think, his first year of teaching. And he did not have any method for controlling the students.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So one day, he brought a bunny to class, but the other students decided that it would be much more entertaining to use the bunny as a soccer ball. So they would just kick the bunny around while the teacher sort of ran around the classroom, trying to stop this. The bunny survived, but it looked like he'd gone blind. One of his eyes was completely mangled.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: In those first few months, Emir made just a single friend, another Bosnian refugee named Emil. Emir and Emil were inseparable, but they were joined mainly by their fear of everyone else.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And how is your English at this point?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Terrible.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: That was another problem. He says he couldn't really talk to the other kids or his teachers, and so he sort of walked around the school in silence, like a mute. To improve his English, he returned to The Fortress, the novel he'd stolen from the Croatian library. At night, he'd sit down with a dictionary and translate The Fortress from Bosnian to English.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: It was useful because it did improve my English, and it also gave me the sense of sort of-- it made me feel literary. It made me feel like I was creating something beautiful.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So he was back to sitting alone in his room with his novel. But as Emir tells it, all of this really just set the stage for his biggest stroke of luck, the one that would not only get him into college, but would change his entire life. It came in the form of a teacher who descended for maybe two weeks upon his English classroom. Emir remembers only her last name, Ames, Miss Ames. Or maybe it was Mrs. Ames.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: He thinks she was an intern training to be a teacher. Anyway, she wasn't around for very long. Unlike his regular teacher, she was full of energy. She tried all these new tricks to engage their interest.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: One day, she handed out these photographs to the kids. The one she gave to Emir was of a boy with a haunted look on his face, looking over his shoulder. Then she told them all to write an essay about the pictures.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Write an essay-- that's a pretty difficult thing for me, given my limited knowledge of English. So first thought, I'm going to dread this task. But then I realized, there's this really beautiful passage, this beautiful chapter I had translated, I had worked on the previous night from The Fortress. So I decide to, pretty much, word for word replicate this passage and use that as my essay for Miss Ames.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I still remember a little bit about what the passage was about. The protagonist has witnessed an injustice. I remember I closed my essay with this bit of internal monologue, which roughly says, "I'm slowly becoming a repository for decomposing sorrows, regrets, ignored injustice, forgotten promises. I can still feel its stench. But when I get accustomed to it, I will call it experience." And I think Miss Ames was impressed.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And since The Fortress had never been translated into English, there was exactly zero chance she'd ever catch him.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: What happened is, the next day, Miss Ames walks up to me and pretty much whispers into my ear, you have to get out of this school, which is not what you typically expect teachers to tell you in school. But I'm like, yeah, where? Where do I go?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: And she said, well, you know, there are private schools. I was like, well, don't those cost money? She says, well, some of them have financial aid. In fact, I have a job interview at a very nice private school on Monday. Why don't you just come with me and ask whether they have financial aid? And I was like, OK.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So the following Monday, instead of going to Clarkston High in the morning, Miss Ames comes to pick me up at our apartment complex. And she drives me to midtown Atlanta to this just beautiful, wonderful school with manicured lawns. It just looks lovely.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: This new place is called The Paideia School. He's never heard of it.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So she goes to have her job interview, and I go to the admissions office. And there's the admissions officer. So she's sort of looking at me as sort of, so? And I remember pretty distinctly, I said, I am a Bosnian refugee. My school is really bad. Can I please go here?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: You'd memorized that sentence?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I think I had practiced it ahead of time. So it's stuck in my head because I had kind of planned this great pitch that I had, which is, I'm a Bosnian refugee. My school is really bad. Can I please go here?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: She points out to me that applications were due three months ago. She asked whether I need financial aid. I asked how much it would be. She said something, which to me, was equivalent to a bazillion dollars. So I said, yes, I need financial aid. She points out those were given out six months ago.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: She then suggests maybe I should think about applying for the following year. And to that, I retort, I'm a Bosnian refugee. My school is really, really bad. Can I please, please go here? And I guess that was effective, particularly in conjunction with the essay, which Miss Ames brought to her job interview, so that when she was asked why she wanted to be a teacher, she pulls out this essay and says, because of children like these.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: These children who plagiarize essays from stolen library books.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: She didn't know that.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Unbeknownst to me at the time, Paideia is the most PC, diversity-obsessed school south of the Mason-Dixon line. I mean, they really think diversity is important. And a Bosnian refugee, at this time, now that's a very rare commodity. So they basically managed to dig up some money.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I was there sophomore, junior, and senior year of high school. And it was a lovely place. It was a heaven on earth, as far as I was concerned. All the teachers went by their first names. We had couches instead of desks in the classrooms. I mean, not just was the school good, I also felt safe. And this feeling of safety had been lacking for the previous few years.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: And I think it does something to you. I think you have new resources to pay attention to things about the world which are beautiful, things about the world which are interesting, things about the world which are intriguing. I'm speculating here, but I think you're somewhere, at a deep level, distracted by the threat. I could instead focus on catching up on the things I hadn't learned.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Four years later, he was a student at Harvard on a scholarship that paid for tuition, room, and board. From there, he went and got his PhD in economics, also from Harvard. At Harvard, he met his future wife. And from Harvard, he went to the University of Chicago, which gave him tenure at a young age. And he's now a rising star in the field of behavioral economics, all because Miss Ames read his plagiarized essay and was fooled by it.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I mean, it is by far the-- in everyone's life, there are many forks. This is by far the biggest one. This has made the most difference. I mean, there's no doubt that my life got onto a very different kind of a track.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: And I'm pretty sure that if it hadn't been for her, I would have stayed in Clarkston High School. I wouldn't have thought to apply to a private school. I most certainly wouldn't have gone to Harvard. And she gave me a piece of paper and a pen 10 years ago and said, OK, describe what you think of as the most wonderful life. I think I'd come up with something less good than what it actually is.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: It's always hard to say how your life would have turned out differently if something hadn't happened to you. But in Emir's case, there's at least one useful reference point, his Bosnian friend, Emil. Emil hadn't been airlifted out of Clarkston into some fancy private school. Instead, he dropped out of Clarkston, done some bad things, and actually spent some time in jail. Eventually, he went back to Bosnia-- no Miss Ames, no rescue.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Over the years, Emir's told this story a lot. It might be his favorite story that he tells about himself. It rhymes with his view of the world, that there's just this huge, accidental component to life's outcomes, that everyone owes at least some of their success not just to chance, but to other people being nice for no reason at all.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: What became of Miss Ames?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I don't know. Turned out she didn't get the job at Paideia, so I never saw her again at Paideia. In fact, I never saw her again.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: At some point, the fact that Emir had no idea what had happened to this woman who'd changed his entire life started to bother him. It's as if the more he told the story, the more grateful he became. And the more grateful he became, the more he wanted to find her, to thank her, but also just to show her the life he had because of her.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: He Googled around for her, but then realized he didn't have any idea how to spell her name. He pestered both of his old schools, but neither of them had any record of her. No one even remembered her. His investigations, such as they were, were sort of half-assed, but what was he going to do? Hire a private eye?

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: My name is Irving Botwinick, and my business is called Serving by Irving.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So you specialize in finding people?

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: That's what we do. We dig them up. Actually, we have a motto. If they're alive, we serve them. If they're dead, we'll tell you where they're buried.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Irving's a private detective who serves lots of court papers. Since Emir wasn't going to hire one, This American Life did it for him.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: All right, so we have somebody we need to find.

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: All right. [CLEARS THROAT] So the person that I'd like to find is called Miss Ames. Not sure how to spell that. I have reasons to think, I can mention later, that she was married, at least the last time I saw her, which was in 1993 in Atlanta, Georgia.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Emir went on to explain in great detail that he knew basically nothing about her-- height, weight, eye color, all a mystery. When Irving asked him what she looked like, he said, quote, "She was neither particularly skinny, nor fat. Not particularly short, nor tall. She looked normal," he said. About the only thing he remembers about her is what she'd done for him. Irving thought the full-time English teacher would be a good place to start, but Emir didn't remember her name either.

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: Did you have a class book for that year?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Oh, no. No.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Somehow, Irving seemed to find what Emir was saying useful. He wrote little notes to himself about what I do not know. But at the top of the page, he wrote Miss Ames. Then he wrote a big question mark. Then he asked Emir to go away and write down everything he could remember from that period of his life. But before he lifted a finger to find Miss Ames he said, he needed to do a character check on Emir.

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: Because a lot of times, investigators get cases where they're trying to track somebody down, and then they go and they kill them. So we have to sort of verify what you're telling us is the truth as well.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So Irving, let's just assume that the facts are as bare as they sound. Is it hopeless?

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: No. There's nobody I can't find, I'll put it that way. I could have found Osama bin Laden if they paid me enough to do it.

segments.text: So how long do you need to do your search? When can we expect to be sitting down in a room with Miss Ames?

segments.speaker: Irving Botwinick
segments.text: Oh, probably before the end of the month, before the end of February.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: The end of February came and went. March came and went too, without the slightest trace of Miss Ames. It wasn't for lack of trying. Irving had put his best agent on the case, a woman named Gabriela Galindo. The first thing Gabriela did was to try the public school, but only two teachers who had been there in 1993 were still around.

segments.speaker: Gabriela Galindo
segments.text: And they had no recollection of not even the English teacher, not even the English teacher.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: She hired a local detective to go to Clarkston to get the yearbook, but they wouldn't give him one. She learned that the Georgia Department of Education keeps a list of all the teachers ever certified in the state, but she couldn't get access to the list. She called nearby colleges to search lists of graduates from the 1990s, still no sign of Miss Ames. Out of desperation, she hunted down all the old phone books from the region from the 1990s.

segments.speaker: Gabriela Galindo
segments.text: These are copies of the phone books that we received going back from 1990 to 1993 of all the people in the greater Atlanta area with the last name Ames, which is a very, very common name, we found.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Gabriela Galindo
segments.text: Very common.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And roughly, how many people were there?

segments.speaker: Gabriela Galindo
segments.text: Oh, my god. Oh, hundreds.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And you weren't even sure her name was Ames.

segments.speaker: Gabriela Galindo
segments.text: Correct. That's the other thing. That's the other thing. We weren't sure.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: They called every Ames on the list, all these hundreds of names. Still didn't find her. And it was starting to feel just a little bit weird. A lot of the people Irving goes hunting for don't want to be found, but he finds them anyway. Here was someone with no obvious reason not to want to be found, and she'd vanished without a trace.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: After a couple of months of this, you couldn't help but wonder, why was this woman the most difficult person on Earth to find? Was it because she wasn't an earthly creature? Not once, but twice this boy had found himself in a world more intent on destroying him than in building him up. Maybe he needed evidence that people weren't all bad. Maybe that's where angels always come from.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Is this Miss Ames?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Yes, it is.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Oh, my goodness. It's like finding a ghost, finding you. It's a pleasure to hear your voice.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: It's just the two of us talking. Emir isn't in the conversation yet.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: I'm going to call you Miss Ames, because I don't want to think of you as anything but Miss Ames.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: I'd much rather be thought of as Lauren. It's a lot sexier.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Well, you know, we didn't actually think of you as a sex object when we were thinking of Miss Ames. We thought of you as an angel coming out of the sky.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Well, that's good too.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Here's how they found her. Gabriela finally got her hands on that list of all the teachers certified in the state of Georgia. She noticed one of the women named Ames had allowed her certification to lapse. This one Ames, she tracked down in West Virginia and left messages for her saying only that she was looking for an English teacher on behalf of a former student.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: And I immediately knew. She didn't mention Emir's name. I just knew. It never crossed my mind that it would be anybody but Emir, frankly. I mean, I knew one day he'd be a famous something.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: The basic plan was to fly Miss Ames to Chicago to meet Emir, but I wanted to ask her what she remembered before Emir had a chance to tell her what she should remember. She told me that she was 36 years old when she arrived at Clarkston High as a student teacher. She'd recently married a man named Chris Ames, and they decided they wouldn't have children of their own. She thinks that maybe the faint regrets of that decision made her want to go out of her way to help some kid.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Anyway, she noticed this extremely talented boy in her class and watched him, not for two weeks as an intern, as Emir had told me, but for many months, an entire semester in which she was put in charge of his class, she says, as his full-time English teacher. And how was Emir's English at the time?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: It was tremendous. It was absolutely tremendous, really, really good.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: There were other differences in their stories. For example, Emir said the public school was terrifying and useless. Miss Ames didn't agree.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Well certainly, there were drugs. And I'm sure there was some violence, but it wasn't a ghetto school. No, it was a quirky, quasi-city, quasi-suburban school that had a great student body that was interesting because they were from so many different places.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: By that, she means from all over the world-- Kenya, Somalia, Bosnia, Vietnam, Korea. The place was like a teenage UN, in her telling. But the most glaring gap between their two stories was a central plot point, the key moment, the plagiarized essay. In Emir's version, it's what saves him. But Miss Ames doesn't even remember it. She recalls the moment she decided to move him to private school this way.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Well, actually, I think it was the day that he diagrammed sentences for me on the blackboard for the rest of the students. [LAUGHS] I couldn't, for the life of me, figure out how to make them learn it. And it was just mind-numbingly boring.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: And Emir said to me, you know, I really think I can explain this, and they'll understand it. So he took over. And it was a great class, and he did a wonderful job. And it just occurred to me, right there on the spot, this kid is just capable of so much more than this school can offer him.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Still, no essay. I give her a little nudge.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: And do you remember any particular piece of work he did? When you think back of his work as a student, did anything in particular catch your attention?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: He wrote an essay about losing his dad in Bosnia and his family coming to America. That was incredibly moving and beautifully written.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Huh. It sounds like a different essay, but at least it's an essay. But as soon as she brings up the essay, she drops it.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: We took a stab, I remember, at poetry in that class, and he was very good at that. He understood meter right away. But I did speak with his math and science teachers, and they said that he was working at a level that was beyond anything that was taught, even in the senior year at the AP level, and that they just were trying to find things to give him to do because he was just so advanced.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: The essay on which Emir has based his entire life story had nothing to do with her decision to help him. That much was clear. It was also clear that Miss Ames hadn't grabbed him on some mistaken whim, but only after observing his rare combination of genius and kindness for months. And then she'd gone and created a battle plan to move him out of public school and into private. She didn't ever have any job interview at the private school. She thinks maybe she told him that just to avoid getting his hopes up.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: I had done a lot of investigation. I met with my colleagues over there, and sent records over, and made a lot of sales pitches, and was told that there may not be enough scholarship money. It was kind of late, this and that, but I kept pushing and pushing. And finally, we got him an appointment over there.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: It isn't just the details that conflict here, it's the whole moral of the story. Miss Ames doesn't believe for a minute that she made all that much of a difference to Emir. She thinks he was so ridiculously gifted that he would've gone on to greater things, even if he'd stayed at Clarkston.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Well, you know, frankly, he didn't even need to go to high school. He could have gone straight to college. He just needed to grow up. I mean, I'm not joking. I just don't think any teacher would get another student like Emir in a lifetime. I had my once-in-a-lifetime student right off the bat.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Did you feel any impulse to get back in touch with him?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: No, let the chicks fly. I'm not really a kid person. Sorry. [LAUGHS] No. You know, we had our own lives, and I wanted him to have his life. And I didn't earn his way into Paideia or Harvard, he did it. It's his accomplishment.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: What happens when the story a person is telling about his life gets fact checked? I don't mean what happens when you say you graduated from college when you actually didn't. And your employer finds out, and you get fired. I mean, what happens when you really want to believe your life story was this. And then you get told by someone who knows better, nope, actually it wasn't this, it was that?

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: You swear you haven't called him?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: No, I wouldn't do-- I'm honest.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: I know you're honest.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A few weeks later, Miss Ames and I meet up in Chicago. We're visiting Emir at his job at the University of Chicago Business School. Up until the time she got our call, the only way Miss Ames has even tried to keep track of Emir is by checking the list of Nobel Prize winners each year to see if his name is on it. And oddly enough, it's not a totally crazy way to try to keep track of him. He hasn't gotten the Nobel Prize yet, but he's the sort of person who might. His colleagues say he's brilliant, and half of them already have gotten the Nobel Prize.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Excuse me, where can we get an elevator to the fifth floor?

segments.text: The Chicago Business School feels less like a school than the headquarters of a highly successful corporation or maybe a Swiss resort.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: This way. There he is.

segments.text: Hi.

segments.text: Hello--

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: --gorgeous.

segments.text: OK. And at that point, we have to take a break. What happens when Emir and Miss Ames sit down and compare notes about his past? Michael Lewis will be back with that in just one minute, from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.text: We eventually settle into Emir's office and turn our attention to Emir's memories, which, thanks to Miss Ames, are suddenly a little problematic themselves. He tells his story all over again until he gets to what he sees as its biggest turning point.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: So I try to put down, to the extent which I could, word for word, this beautiful passage from this accomplished writer.

segments.text: He doesn't change any of the facts, but his tone is just a tiny bit less certain, maybe because he sees Miss Ames writhing in her chair.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: Yeah. I mouthed to you, he plagiarized it. I'm horrified.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: I'm truly horrified. No one wants to be duped.

segments.text: Here's the safest way to plagiarize-- do it in the distant past. The teacher is no longer capable of getting angry about it, and the plagiarist is no longer even faintly embarrassed. But Miss Ames is now shaking her head.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: It didn't happen that fast, though. It was April when we went. You know, I'd already worked with you for a couple of months when we went in to see--

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Do you remember that?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: --to see the people at Paideia. I'd seen a lot more work than just one essay. And seeing what he could do in class on a daily basis was more impressive to me.

segments.text: It's about now that Emir begins to see that Miss Ames is screwing up his life story. The plagiarized essay is the key to the thing. And he doesn't want it to be about something else.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I recognize that my memory of it is somewhat spotty, but I do have what seems like a pretty distinct memory of the essay sort of triggering the conversation that, you should get out of this school, followed very closely on the heels--

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: It may have, but I was already convinced.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: --of the essay.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I remember the racial mix as being very few-- I remember being one of 12 white kids in a school of 900. That's not right?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: I think it was probably more 40% African American, 40% international and kids from all over the world. And about 20% of the kids were white kids who were longtime Clarkston residents. Family after family lived there.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: That's certainly not my recollection. But then again, this is a matter for research rather than debate. It's probably easy to check.

segments.text: Here it is, a single objective fact that they disagree about that can be checked, a fact that might shed light on whose version of this story is more strictly true. segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Emir's estimate that he was one of a dozen white kids in the school leaves out, oh, roughly 200 other white kids. They made up 17% of the school, pretty close to Miss Ames' estimate. segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: You would have gotten into the honors program at UGA from Clarkston or gone to Georgia Tech. And from an undergraduate degree in the honors program at UGA or Georgia Tech, you could have gotten into Harvard for a PhD, or Chicago, or Stanford. I mean, it's doable. It happens. I know people who've done it.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: If Emir cares what Miss Ames thinks, he's doing a pretty good job of hiding his interest. It isn't until she describes what happened after she helped him out that he becomes truly excited.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: There were quite a few people at the school who weren't thrilled with the fact that I poached their best student, so they sent me to the absolute worst school in the county and put me under the new principal there, who had been the assistant principal at Clarkston. And he brought me in his office and said, you know, you've got a lot of high-minded ideas, and you don't know what you're talking about, and it's going to be my job to break you in, and you're going to learn how to do this right, and so forth and so on.

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: And it was really rough year. He did break me in. In fact, he broke me because I quit. I couldn't take it anymore.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So he did this because you had poached Emir from the school?

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: To be totally honest with you, yeah.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: For helping Emir to move from the public school to the private school, Miss Ames was more or less driven out of teaching. She quit, changed careers, and eventually moved with her husband to West Virginia, where she's now an interior designer.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I mean, wait. So to get this right, you are telling me not only did you go through all of this trouble, but--

segments.speaker: Miss Ames
segments.text: I told you, this wasn't fair.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: Why is it not fair? It's incredibly important. It transforms what-- you know, this is just changing by the minute from my conceptualization of, you know, well, you know, we-- for two weeks, you said, you should go to this place.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: It was fantastic. It made all the difference. That's enough, because that changed my life. So what I'm learning only now is that you did all of these things, and then that you were basically cast out of the apparent paradise, which is Clarkston, which I still find a little doubling, increasing by an order of magnitude what was already an enormous amount of gratitude.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: That night, Emir invited Miss Ames to his house for dinner and to meet his wife and 18-month-old daughter. He wanted to show her the life that he never would have had if not for her.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: [BABY CRYING]

segments.text: Much, much later, after dinner and drinks, and more drinks, and after he's passed out some stiff cocktail from the old country, I ask Emir how it'll change his life story, now that he's heard what actually happened. But what about the plagiarized essay from the stolen library book on which the whole story turns?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I mean, suppose that the story was-- just let's kind of do a thought experiment-- there was no recollection of the essay, none whatsoever. I wouldn't enjoy telling the story about the essay at that point.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Wait. We don't have to do that thought experiment. That's what really happened. Miss Ames actually didn't remember the essay. Emir's already forgotten that fact.

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I wasn't convinced by the alternative account. Genuinely, because it was so apparent that I was also diagramming sentences, which does make a far worse story, dramatically speaking. I diagrammed this sentence. And boy, you know how well I diagrammed it? It was just fantastic. I mean, the verbs, and the nouns, and the adjectives, and the adverbs were all just separate.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: I didn't really see the point of torturing Emir any further. He needed his story to be what it was, and so he was sticking to it. The question was, why? What did it do for him? Why does a man who makes his career as a scientist cling to his story, in spite of evidence that it isn't true? And that's when it dawns on me, Emir Kamenica is just an unusually happy human being. He exudes the emotion from every pore.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Have you always been happy?

segments.speaker: Emir Kamenica
segments.text: I think I've been happy for a pretty long time now.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Now, there's no obvious connection between a person's happiness and the way he tells stories about himself, but I think there's a not so obvious one. When you insist the way that Emir does that you're both lucky and indebted to other people, well, you're sort of prepared to see life as a happy accident, aren't you? It's just very different than if you tell yourself that you simply deserve all the good stuff that happens to you because you happen to be born a genius, or suffered so much, or worked so hard. That way of telling the story-- well, that's what you hear from every miserable bond trader at Goldman Sachs, or for that matter, every other A-hole who ever walked the earth.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: It's at this exact moment when the subject of happiness comes up that Emir's wife, Yelena, becomes very interested.

segments.speaker: Yelena
segments.text: Both I know it and all of my friends know that he's the happiest person that we've met. You can't fake it. You can't decide that I'm just going to be happy, because it will unravel very quickly. And you will find reasons to be grumpy.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: The reason her husband's so happy, she thinks, has to do with the way he filters the world around him, the way he decides not just what to think about, but how to think about it. She says she sees him do this all the time.

segments.speaker: Yelena
segments.text: It's a micro decision. I've seen him get some news and decide how to feel about that. It's a practiced decision, but I still observed Emir making that decision. And I've tried to crack that code by living with him. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: Crack what code?

segments.speaker: Yelena
segments.text: The code of happiness, making that decision of how you're going to feel about something.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: These stories we tell about ourselves, they're almost like our infrastructure, like railroads or highways. We can build them almost any way we want to. But once they're in place, this whole inner landscape grows up around them.

segments.speaker: Michael Lewis
segments.text: So maybe the point here is that you should be careful about how you tell your story, or at least conscious of it. Because once you've told it, once you've built the highway, it's just very hard to move it. Even if your story is about an angel who came out of nowhere and saved your life, even then, not even the angel herself can change it.
